title: Crimp a tube lug onto a 16 mm² cable in a bench crimping press, then lay the cable back on its rest
instruction: Crimp the cable lug sitting in the crimping press onto the cable's stripped end, then lay the cable, lug on, back on its rest and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Terminating stranded power cables with crimped compression lugs, which then bolt onto breakers, busbars, transformers and motor terminals, is regular work for electricians (about 821,000 US jobs in 2025 per BLS; O*NET tasks "Connect wires to circuit breakers, transformers, or other components" and "Install ground leads and connect power cables to equipment, such as motors") and for electrical and electronic equipment assemblers, control-panel builders among them (246,300 US jobs). The stripped end has to go fully into the lug's barrel and stay straight while the die closes, or the joint fails a pull test or overheats.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A pneumatic lug crimper (iCrimp AM-70, hex type; 510 x 150 x 195 mm, 18 kg: an orange steel housing holding its air cylinder, and steel jaws in front) on the centre line, pointing at the arms: its jaws start 22 cm forward, its housing ends 73 cm forward. The jaws, open (the upper jaw raised 15 degrees), hold its hexagonal die set with the 16 mm2 cavity (die pair G16) centred 27 cm forward, 7.5 cm above the table. (2) In the lower half of that die lies a tinned-copper tubular cable lug for 16 mm2 cable (Klauke 3R8: barrel 5.5 mm inside, 8.5 mm outside and 13 mm long; a flat palm 15 mm wide with an 8.5 mm (M8) hole; 29 mm long, 9 g), its barrel running sideways with its mouth 6.5 mm left of the centre line, its palm to the right with its end against a lug stop (a 24 x 16 x 81 mm block standing on the table). (3) A guard of 3 mm clear polycarbonate encloses the jaws: walls 16 cm tall from 20.5 cm forward back to the housing, 4.8 cm right and 2.75 cm left of the centre line, and a lid. Its left wall, 1.8 cm left of the barrel's mouth, has a 22 mm square feed hole on the barrel's axis. (4) The press's pedal valve (Camozzi 354N-925, 5/2, set to monostable; 246 x 138 mm, a blue body 67.5 mm tall and a yellow cover rising to 152.9 mm at its high end) stands on the table along the forward direction, 24 cm right of the centre line, its hinged low end 53 cm forward and its high end toward the arms. Pressing the flat of its high end (30 cm forward) 2.0 cm down, against 17 N (the maker's actuating force at 6 bar), switches the valve; the cover stops 2.5 cm down. Held down, the valve closes the press's jaws (in 1 s in the simulation); let go, it opens them. Air: a 150 psi shop compressor (Porter-Cable C2002), regulated to 0.75 MPa, feeds the valve, whose two outlets go to the press's two cylinder ports (10 mm tube). (5) A loose 16 mm2 single-core PVC-insulated cable (H07V-R, stiff), 16 cm long, 7 mm across and 27 g, its last 13 mm stripped to its stranded copper conductor, 5.1 mm across (the strip length matching the lug's barrel), lies sideways on two black ABS-plastic V-rests 20 cm forward, its axis 3 cm above the table, its bare tip 9 cm left of the centre line and pointing right. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. The crimp: the moment the press's jaws first close fully (the pedal held down past its switch point for 1 s), which closes the die on the barrel. A good crimp: then the bare end 10.5 to 13.5 mm into the 13 mm barrel (all but at most 2.5 mm of the copper in; the insulation, too wide to enter, stops at the barrel's mouth) and the cable within 8 degrees of the barrel's axis. If the jaws first close with no copper in the barrel, they crush it shut and no crimp can follow. Released: the pedal back up, the jaws open again, and both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) at least 4 cm from the pedal's press point. Taken out: after the crimp, the cable's tip at least 5 cm from where the barrel's mouth was (out through the feed hole), the lug on it. On its rest: the cable's tip within 3 cm (across) and 1.5 cm (up or down) of where it lay, the cable within 20 degrees of lying along the rests. 1.0: a good crimp, released, taken out, laid back on its rest, and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: any crimp with the bare end in the barrel; 0.25: the bare end pushed at least 6.5 mm into the barrel at some point; else 0.0. In a real trial: the crimp shows as the full hexagonal impression of the closed die on the barrel, checked by eye after the trial; the depth is read with a caliper as the bare gap between the insulation's end and the barrel's mouth (a 13 mm strip in a 13 mm barrel: a gap of at most 2.5 mm means at least 10.5 mm in); the cable's angle, the pedal, the jaws, the rest position and the arms are read from the overhead video; and a good crimp must also pass a pull test: the lug holds a steady 450 N pull on the cable (the UL 486A pull-out force for this size). The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the pedal and the cable still.
reset_notes: Let go of the pedal so the jaws open; lift the guard's lid, lay a fresh Klauke 3R8 lug in the lower 16 mm2 die with its palm against the stop, and close the lid; lay a fresh cable, stripped 13 mm with its strands twisted tight, on its rests. Check that the regulator reads 0.75 MPa.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). The crimp is an event: when the jaws have closed, the task file reads where the cable's bare end is and, if it is in the barrel, swaps the lug for a crimped one that then goes where the cable goes (its hold isn't simulated). The cable is a stiff rod; the lug is fixed in the die (really, it rests against its stop). The air cylinder isn't modelled: the valve turns the shown jaw shut in 1 s. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
